"executive_summary": "This paper is a theoretical, argumentative essay rather than an empirical study, so it contains no participants, measurements, or numerical results in the usual sense; its 'results' are logical and physical consequences derived from extrapolating the standard cosmological model forward in time. The authors, Lawrence M. Krauss and Robert J. Scherrer of Case Western Reserve University and Vanderbilt University, argue that as the current Lambda-CDM universe is extrapolated forward, all evidence of Hubble expansion will disappear, so that future observers in our 'island universe' will be fundamentally incapable of determining the true nature of the universe. They identify three observational pillars of modern cosmology—the observed Hubble expansion, the detection of the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and the determination of the abundance of elements produced in the early universe—and describe how each will vanish for a far-future observer. They note that all cosmological models with a non-zero cosmological constant will approach a de Sitter universe in the far future, and they re-examine the practical significance of this ultimate de Sitter expansion, pointing out a new consequence: from the perspective of any observer within a bound gravitational system, the static version of de Sitter space outside that system will eventually become the appropriate physical coordinate system. They argue that in a time comparable to the age of the longest-lived stars, observers will not be able to perform any observation or experiment that infers either an expanding universe dominated by a cosmological constant or a hot Big Bang. Observers will be able to infer a finite age for their island universe, but beyond that cosmology will effectively be over. The authors detail the disappearance of the Hubble expansion, noting that the Local Group remains gravitationally bound while more distant structures are driven outside the de Sitter event horizon on a timescale on the order of 100 billion years, and that light from them is exponentially redshifted so that within a time frame comparable to the longest-lived main sequence stars all objects outside the local cluster become truly invisible. They describe the vanishing CMB, noting that at t approximately 100 Gyr the peak wavelength of the CMB will be redshifted to roughly 1 m or a frequency of roughly 300 MHz, and that the intensity will be redshifted by about 12 orders of magnitude, with the microwave background peak redshifting below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium. They argue that general relativity gives no assistance, because the inference of expansion depends on the assumption of an isotropic and homogeneous universe, which will not hold for future observers. They discuss polluted elemental abundances, noting that the primordial helium mass fraction of Y = 0.25 will be dwarfed by the ultimate mass fraction of helium Y = 0.6, and that relic deuterium will be destroyed. They conclude that we live in a very special time in the evolution of the universe, the time at which we can observationally verify that we live in a very special time. summary.title: The Return of a Static Universe and the End of Cosmology
summary.authors: Lawrence M. Krauss and Robert J. Scherrer
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical/conceptual essay (no empirical data, simulations, or experiments)
summary.executive_summary: This paper is a theoretical, argumentative essay rather than an empirical study, so it contains no participants, measurements, or numerical results in the usual sense; its 'results' are logical and physical consequences derived from extrapolating the standard cosmological model forward in time. The authors, Lawrence M. Krauss and Robert J. Scherrer of Case Western Reserve University and Vanderbilt University, argue that as the current Lambda-CDM universe is extrapolated forward, all evidence of Hubble expansion will disappear, so that future observers in our 'island universe' will be fundamentally incapable of determining the true nature of the universe. They identify three observational pillars of modern cosmology—the observed Hubble expansion, the detection of the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and the determination of the abundance of elements produced in the early universe—and describe how each will vanish for a far-future observer. They note that all cosmological models with a non-zero cosmological constant will approach a de Sitter universe in the far future, and they re-examine the practical significance of this ultimate de Sitter expansion, pointing out a new consequence: from the perspective of any observer within a bound gravitational system, the static version of de Sitter space outside that system will eventually become the appropriate physical coordinate system. They argue that in a time comparable to the age of the longest-lived stars, observers will not be able to perform any observation or experiment that infers either an expanding universe dominated by a cosmological constant or a hot Big Bang. Observers will be able to infer a finite age for their island universe, but beyond that cosmology will effectively be over. The authors detail the disappearance of the Hubble expansion, noting that the Local Group remains gravitationally bound while more distant structures are driven outside the de Sitter event horizon on a timescale on the order of 100 billion years, and that light from them is exponentially redshifted so that within a time frame comparable to the longest-lived main sequence stars all objects outside the local cluster become truly invisible. They describe the vanishing CMB, noting that at t approximately 100 Gyr the peak wavelength of the CMB will be redshifted to roughly 1 m or a frequency of roughly 300 MHz, and that the intensity will be redshifted by about 12 orders of magnitude, with the microwave background peak redshifting below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium. They argue that general relativity gives no assistance, because the inference of expansion depends on the assumption of an isotropic and homogeneous universe, which will not hold for future observers. They discuss polluted elemental abundances, noting that the primordial helium mass fraction of Y = 0.25 will be dwarfed by the ultimate mass fraction of helium Y = 0.6, and that relic deuterium will be destroyed. They conclude that we live in a very special time in the evolution of the universe, the time at which we can observationally verify that we live in a very special time. The paper contains no bibliography, so top_influential_citations is empty, and it reports no data, code, or ethics information, so those fields are empty.
